query: Which material can be used for superconducting properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: High-temperature superconductors based on cuprates will exhibit superconducting properties at temperatures above 90 K.
generation.material_initial_state: Cuprate materials in their normal state at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Cooling the cuprate materials to below their critical temperature.
generation.conditions: Under an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation and at varying pressures to observe effects on superconductivity.
generation.structural_mediator: The layered structure of cuprate materials, which facilitates electron pairing.
generation.mechanism: Electron pairing mediated by lattice vibrations (phonons) in the presence of strong electron correlations.
generation.predicted_outcome: The cuprate materials will transition to a superconducting state, exhibiting zero electrical resistance and the expulsion of magnetic fields (Meissner effect) at temperatures above 90 K.
generation.baseline: Normal state of cuprate materials at room temperature, which shows no superconducting properties.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is limited to cuprate materials and does not extend to other classes of superconductors.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical temperature may vary based on specific cuprate compositions and external conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Cool a sample of a cuprate material and measure its electrical resistance as temperature decreases.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the material does not exhibit zero resistance or the Meissner effect above 90 K, the hypothesis is falsified.
